packet.evaluation_question: At 36 hours, culture is negative but symptoms persist. Explain the missing criteria for stopping antibiotics.

evidence.text: For babies given antibiotics because of suspected late-onset infection, consider stopping the antibiotics at 48 hours if: • the blood culture is negative and • the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection and • the levels and trends of C‑reactive protein concentration are reassuring. [2021]

Consider establishing hospital systems to provide blood culture results 36 hours after starting antibiotics for early-onset neonatal infection, to allow timely stopping of treatment and discharge from hospital. [2012]

When continuing intravenous antibiotics for longer than 36 hours despite negative blood cultures, review the need for ongoing antibiotics at least once every 24 hours, taking account of: • the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection and • the baby's clinical progress and current condition and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration. [2012] 1.22 Switching to oral antibiotics

For babies born from 35+0 weeks' gestation with negative blood culture who need antibiotics for more than 36 hours because the initial clinical suspicion of infection was strong, consider switching treatment from intravenous to oral antibiotics at 36 hours or thereafter to complete the course (up to 7 days of antibiotics in total) if: • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no current clinical indicators of ongoing infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring and • the baby is tolerating oral feeds. [2026]

reasons: C1: Claim that clinical condition is not reassuring due to undocumented criteria is not entailed by evidence; evidence only states criteria for reassurance, not that lack of documentation implies non-reassurance.
C2: Evidence E3 advises reviewing need for ongoing antibiotics, not that antibiotics must be continued because suspicion is strong; claim overstates guidance.
C3: Frequency of monitoring (every 12h) is not specified in evidence; only that CRP trends are relevant, so monitoring plan is unsupported.
C4: Specific escalation thresholds (RR >70, SpO2 <94%) are not mentioned in evidence; claim introduces unsupported criteria.
C5: Evidence E1 pertains to stopping antibiotics for suspected late-onset infection and does not address parent communication; claim is unsupported.
C6: Evidence E1 addresses late-onset infection stopping at 48h, not early-onset neonatal sepsis; applying it to this patient is wrong population.

C1: The claim infers that the clinical condition is not reassuring because documentation is missing; the guideline only states that reassurance is required for stopping, not that missing documentation equals non‑reassurance.
C2: The guideline advises reviewing the need for ongoing antibiotics, taking suspicion into account, but does not explicitly mandate continuation of IV antibiotics; the claim overstates the guidance.

C3: The guideline mentions monitoring CRP trends as part of the reassurance criteria, but does not specify a 12‑hour monitoring interval for respiratory rate or SpO2; the claim adds unsupported details.
C4: The escalation thresholds (RR >70, SpO2 <94%) are not present in the cited evidence; the claim introduces criteria not found in the guideline.
C5: The cited evidence describes criteria for stopping antibiotics, not communication content with parents; the claim is not directly supported.
